gate_validation.artifact: The v1.7 benchmark evaluated 20 systems on 5 algorithmic tasks, scoring each against 133 visible checks and 63 hidden checks [S1]. Its central result concerns a gated pool of low-cost models climbing against a machine gate [S1]. The gated pool scored 100% on visible checks and 98% on hidden checks [S1]. It reached that score at an average task cost of $0.032 [S1]. The strongest frontier lane matched that correctness only at 6 to 29 times the cost [S1]. The same pool run without a gate scored 88% on visible checks and 84% on hidden checks [S1]. That contrast is the headline: the lift comes from the gate, not from the models [S1]. An objective re-score normalized formatting with an auto-formatter before measuring anything else [S2]. After that normalization the gated pool recorded the highest maintainability index in the fold, at 51.6 [S2]. It also recorded the fastest measured runtime in the fold, at 103 ms [S2]. It did so with zero high-severity security findings [S2]. Judge preferences for frontier output were driven mostly by formatting rather than substance [S2]. The benchmark also recorded its own limits with unusual candor [S3]. All tasks were single-file Python algorithms, so the results may not transfer to multi-file or non-code work [S3]. The gates were authored by the benchmark operators themselves and validated against reference solutions and known-bad mutants [S3]. A multi-round polish stage was tested and rejected [S3]. That polish stage reduced hidden-check correctness from 100% to 93% even as it raised judge scores [S3]. The operators also state plainly that the verification gates are not tamper-proof against adversarial submissions [S3]. Taken together, the benchmark establishes that a machine gate converts low-cost model output into frontier-grade correctness at a small fraction of the cost [S1]. Its evidence base remains narrow, and the honest limits it records are the right frame for reading the headline numbers [S3].

cells.artifact: The v1.7 benchmark provided the first systematic, head-to-head comparison of a gated cheap-model execution strategy against frontier single-model approaches across twenty evaluated systems, all measured on five discrete algorithmic tasks [S1]. The evaluation harness applied a rigorous dual-layer checking protocol consisting of 133 visible checks and 63 hidden checks to prevent surface-level gaming of the results [S1]. Under this protocol, the gated cheap-model pool achieved a perfect 100 percent score on the visible checks and a 98 percent score on the hidden checks, demonstrating that the gating mechanism successfully filtered and corrected outputs before final submission [S1]. In direct contrast, the strongest frontier lane matched that correctness level only at a cost that was six to twenty-nine times higher, while the same cheap-model pool operating without a gate saw its performance collapse to 88 percent visible and 84 percent hidden correctness [S1]. This established that a gate-first architecture could decouple raw model capability from delivered reliability and cost by intercepting low-quality responses before they reached the check stage [S1]. The average task cost for the gated cheap-model pool was just $0.032, making it radically cheaper than the frontier alternatives for equivalent or superior accuracy [S1]. An objective re-score process later stripped away surface-level formatting biases by running all outputs through an auto-formatter and then measuring lint issues, security findings, cyclomatic complexity, maintainability index, and actual runtime performance [S2]. In that re-score, the gated pool recorded the highest maintainability index in the entire fold at 51.6 and the fastest execution runtime at 103 milliseconds, alongside zero high-severity security findings [S2]. The re-score further revealed that the original LLM-judge preferences, which had often favored frontier models, were driven predominantly by formatting rather than by substantive code quality or correctness [S2]. These findings collectively established that a gated, multi-model pipeline could not only match but often surpass monolithic frontier systems on pure algorithmic merit while slashing computational costs [S1][S2]. The benchmark’s scope, however, was deliberately narrow, as all tasks were limited to single-file Python algorithms, which means the observed benefits may not transfer to multi-file projects, repository-scale engineering, or non-code domains such as prose generation [S3]. Another critical architectural constraint was that the verification gates were authored by the benchmark operators themselves and validated solely against reference solutions and a collection of known-bad mutants, thus they embodied operator-defined rather than automatically derived correctness criteria [S3]. The gates were explicitly not tamper-proof against adversarial submissions, so they cannot guarantee robustness in a setting where a model actively tries to circumvent the checks [S3]. An additional experimental finding further circumscribed the technique’s applicability, since a multi-round LLM polish stage was tested as an enhancement and rejected because it degraded hidden-check correctness from the original 100 percent down to 93 percent, even while it paradoxically raised LLM-judge scores [S3]. Consequently, the benchmark established that a single-pass gated workflow with static checks is currently superior to iterative LLM-driven refinement for these algorithmic tasks, but it also highlighted that surface-level evaluation metrics and human-preference scores can be actively misleading proxies for hidden functional correctness [S2][S3]. The overall outcome is a qualified proof that gate-first execution with small models can match frontier quality at a fraction of the cost under controlled, single-file coding conditions, yet the approach remains untested and unverified beyond that tightly bounded experimental frame [S1][S3].

The 2026 v1.7 benchmark evaluated 20 systems across 5 algorithmic tasks using 133 visible and 63 hidden checks [S1]. Within this setup, a gated cheap-model pool achieved 100% accuracy on visible checks and 98% on hidden checks, at an average task cost of $0.032 [S1]. The strongest frontier lane matched this correctness but did so at 6 to 29 times the cost of the gated cheap pool [S1]. When the same cheap-model pool was run without a gate, performance dropped to 88% on visible checks and 84% on hidden checks, indicating the gate itself was responsible for a substantial correctness gain [S1]. This establishes that gating cheap models can approach or match frontier-lane correctness while dramatically reducing cost [S1]. Beyond correctness, an objective re-score was conducted to assess code quality independent of surface style [S2]. This re-score normalized formatting using an auto-formatter, then measured lint issues, security findings, cyclomatic complexity, maintainability index, and actual runtime [S2]. The gated pool achieved the highest maintainability index in the fold at 51.6 and the fastest runtime at 103 ms, alongside zero high-severity security findings [S2]. Notably, LLM-judge preferences that favored frontier-model output were found to be driven mostly by formatting differences rather than substantive code quality [S2]. Together, these findings suggest that gated cheap-model pools not only match correctness cost-effectively but also produce maintainable, performant, and secure code, undermining judge-based preferences that reward superficial polish [S1][S2]. However, the benchmark has explicit limits that constrain generalization [S3]. The evaluated tasks were restricted to single-file Python algorithmic problems, so results may not transfer to multi-file projects or non-code work [S3]. The verification gates themselves were authored by the benchmark operators, who validated them against reference solutions and known-bad mutants, meaning gate quality depends on the operators' own judgment and test design [S3]. A multi-round LLM polish stage was also tested and subsequently rejected as part of the benchmark design, because it reduced hidden-check correctness from 100% to 93% even though it raised judge scores [S3]. This rejection reinforces the broader finding that judge-based scoring can diverge from actual correctness [S2][S3]. Finally, the benchmark's authors acknowledge that the verification gates are not tamper-proof against adversarial submissions, leaving open the possibility that a system could game the gates without producing genuinely correct or high-quality code [S3]. Taken together, the benchmark establishes strong evidence that gating is a cost-effective mechanism for achieving frontier-level correctness and code quality with cheap models on constrained algorithmic tasks [S1][S2], while simultaneously flagging that this evidence is scoped to single-file Python problems, dependent on operator-authored gates, and vulnerable to adversarial gaming [S3].
